name: Prophets and Exile
opening_note: When Israel's kings failed — and most of them did — God did not go silent. He sent prophets. This arc walks through God's voice across roughly three hundred years of slow national decline, ending in exile in Babylon. The prophets weren't fortune-tellers. They were the conscience of a forgetful nation. They wept, they thundered, they pleaded, they promised. All of them were saying versions of the same thing: come back.
closing_note: The Old Testament closes with a promise — a messenger is coming, and a Day of the Lord with him. Then silence. For roughly four hundred years, no prophet speaks. The next arc, "Return and Waiting," covers what happened during those silent centuries — the return from exile, the rebuilding of Jerusalem, and the long quiet years in which, without anyone fully realizing it, the world was being prepared for the coming of Jesus.

blocks.text: So Ahab sent to all the children of Israel, and gathered the prophets together to Mount Carmel.
Elijah came near to all the people, and said, "How long will you waver between the two sides? If Yahweh is God, follow him; but if Baal, then follow him." The people didn't say a word.
Then Elijah said to the people, "I, even I only, am left as a prophet of Yahweh; but Baal's prophets are four hundred fifty men.

Let them therefore give us two bulls; and let them choose one bull for themselves, and cut it in pieces, and lay it on the wood, and put no fire under; and I will dress the other bull, and lay it on the wood, and put no fire under it.
You call on the name of your god, and I will call on Yahweh's name. The God who answers by fire, let him be God." All the people answered, "It is well said."
Elijah said to the prophets of Baal, "Choose one bull for yourselves, and dress it first; for you are many; and call on the name of your god, but put no fire under it."

They took the bull which was given them, and they dressed it, and called on the name of Baal from morning even until noon, saying, "Baal, hear us!" But there was no voice, and nobody answered. They leaped about the altar which was made.
At noon, Elijah mocked them, and said, "Cry aloud; for he is a god. Either he is musing, or he has gone aside, or he is on a journey, or perhaps he sleeps and must be awakened."
They cried aloud, and cut themselves in their way with knives and lances, until the blood gushed out on them.
When midday was past, they prophesied until the time of the evening offering; but there was no voice, no answer, and nobody paid attention.
Elijah said to all the people, "Come near to me!" All the people came near to him. He repaired Yahweh's altar that had been thrown down.
Elijah took twelve stones, according to the number of the tribes of the sons of Jacob, to whom Yahweh's word came, saying, "Israel shall be your name."
With the stones he built an altar in Yahweh's name. He made a trench around the altar, large enough to contain two seahs of seed.
He put the wood in order, and cut the bull in pieces, and laid it on the wood. He said, "Fill four jars with water, and pour it on the burnt offering, and on the wood."
He said, "Do it a second time;" and they did it the second time. He said, "Do it a third time;" and they did it the third time.
The water ran around the altar; and he also filled the trench with water.

At the time of the evening offering, Elijah the prophet came near, and said, "Yahweh, the God of Abraham, of Isaac, and of Israel, let it be known today that you are God in Israel, and that I am your servant, and that I have done all these things at your word.
Hear me, Yahweh, hear me, that this people may know that you, Yahweh, are God, and that you have turned their heart back again."
Then Yahweh's fire fell, and consumed the burnt offering, the wood, the stones, and the dust, and licked up the water that was in the trench.
When all the people saw it, they fell on their faces. They said, "Yahweh, he is God! Yahweh, he is God!"
Elijah said to them, "Seize the prophets of Baal! Don't let one of them escape!" They seized them; and Elijah brought them down to the brook Kishon, and killed them there.
When Yahweh was about to take Elijah up by a whirlwind into heaven, Elijah went with Elisha from Gilgal.
Elijah said to Elisha, "Please wait here, for Yahweh has sent me as far as Bethel." Elisha said, "As Yahweh lives, and as your soul lives, I will not leave you." So they went down to Bethel.
Elijah said to him, "Please wait here, for Yahweh has sent me to the Jordan." He said, "As Yahweh lives, and as your soul lives, I will not leave you." So they both went on.
Elijah took his mantle, and rolled it up, and struck the waters; and they were divided here and there, so that they both went over on dry ground.
When they had gone over, Elijah said to Elisha, "Ask what I shall do for you, before I am taken from you." Elisha said, "Please let a double portion of your spirit be on me."
As they continued on and talked, behold, a chariot of fire and horses of fire separated them; and Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven.
Elisha saw it, and he cried, "My father, my father, the chariots of Israel and its horsemen!" He saw him no more. Then he took hold of his own clothes, and tore them in two pieces.
He took up Elijah's mantle that fell from him, and went back, and stood by the bank of the Jordan.

He took Elijah's mantle that fell from him, and struck the waters, and said, "Where is Yahweh, the God of Elijah?" When he also had struck the waters, they were divided here and there; and Elisha went over.
When the sons of the prophets who were at Jericho facing him saw him, they said, "The spirit of Elijah rests on Elisha." They fell to the ground before him.

days.context_before:
Yesterday's arc ended with the kingdom split in two — Israel in the north, Judah in the south — and most of the kings failing. Today you'll meet the other voice God uses when the kings go wrong: the prophet.

Before the writing prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah, the books with their names on them), there were the speaking prophets. Two stand out from the worst years of the northern kingdom: Elijah and his successor Elisha. Today's reading drops you into the most famous scene from Elijah's life — a public showdown with the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel — and then the strange, glorious moment where Elijah is taken up to heaven and Elisha picks up his cloak.

First, a framework. A prophet in the Bible is not a fortune-teller. The Hebrew word *nabi* means roughly "spokesperson." A prophet speaks for God — usually to call God's people back when they've wandered. The prophets you'll meet this week mostly came when the kings were failing. They're the conscience of a forgetful nation.

Watch for Elijah's question in verse 21: "How long will you waver between two sides?" That single sentence is what the next six days are about.
days.plain_english_simple:
Israel's king Ahab and his wife Jezebel had pushed the worship of a foreign god named Baal across the country. Most of God's prophets had been hunted down. Elijah is one of the few left.

He sets up a public contest on Mount Carmel. Two altars. Two bulls. Baal's prophets call on Baal. Elijah calls on Yahweh. Whichever god sends fire from heaven is the real God.

Baal's 450 prophets cry out all morning. They dance. They cut themselves with knives. Nothing happens. At noon Elijah mocks them — maybe your god is busy, maybe he's asleep.

Then Elijah rebuilds the broken altar of Yahweh. He soaks the wood in water — three times — until the whole altar is drowning. He prays a short prayer. Fire falls from heaven and consumes everything — the bull, the wood, the stones, even the water in the trench. The people fall on their faces: "Yahweh, he is God!"

Later, Elijah's time on earth comes to a close. He and his successor Elisha walk to the Jordan. Elijah strikes the water with his cloak; it parts. Then a chariot of fire and horses of fire come down, and Elijah is taken up to heaven in a whirlwind. Elisha picks up the fallen cloak, strikes the water — and it parts again.

God's voice did not leave Israel. The cloak just passed to a new shoulder.
days.plain_english_standard:
Today introduces the prophets — and the two most famous prophets from before the writing prophets: Elijah and Elisha. To make sense of what follows this week, you need a working definition.

**What is a prophet?** The Hebrew word *nabi* essentially means "spokesperson." A prophet speaks for God to people, especially when those people have wandered. Prophets do sometimes predict future events — but prediction is a small part of the job. The much larger part is *calling God's people back*. The prophets are God's voice when the kings stop listening.

Most of the prophets you'll read about this week ministered between roughly 850 BC and 430 BC — the long arc of Israel's decline, the split kingdoms, the fall of the north (722 BC), the fall of the south (586 BC), and the exile. They are not in chronological order in your Bible. They are grouped by length (major / minor) and not by date. This week we'll walk them in roughly the order they actually spoke.

**Elijah on Mount Carmel.** Elijah comes early in this story — around 870 BC, during the reign of the wicked King Ahab of the northern kingdom. Ahab's wife Jezebel had imported the worship of Baal, a Canaanite storm god believed to control rain and fertility. Israel was wavering between Yahweh and Baal — trying to keep both, committed to neither.

Elijah's challenge in verse 21 is the heart of the chapter: "How long will you waver between the two sides?" The Hebrew word for "waver" literally means to limp or hobble on two crutches. Israel was spiritually limping — uncommitted to either God.

The contest is theater with stakes. Baal supposedly controlled fire and lightning. If anyone could send fire from heaven, Baal should be able to. His 450 prophets call on him all morning. They dance, they shout, they cut themselves. Nothing happens.

Elijah's mockery in verse 27 is biting — and worth noticing. The Hebrew suggests Baal might be "relieving himself" — a bathroom joke at the expense of the rival god. The Bible's prophets are not always solemn. Sometimes they expose idols by ridicule.

Then Elijah builds his altar. Twelve stones — one for each tribe of Israel, including the tribes of the divided north and south, a quiet reminder of what the people once were. He drowns the wood with water. He prays one short prayer. Fire falls and consumes everything.

The people respond: "Yahweh, he is God!" The story makes its point — Yahweh is real, Baal is not.

**The passing of the mantle.** The second passage jumps ahead. Elijah's ministry is ending. He walks with his successor Elisha to the Jordan, strikes the water with his cloak, and they cross on dry ground (a deliberate echo of Moses at the Red Sea and Joshua at the Jordan). A chariot of fire and horses of fire descend, and Elijah is taken up to heaven in a whirlwind — one of only two people in the Bible (the other is Enoch in Genesis 5) who don't experience normal death.

Elisha picks up Elijah's fallen cloak — the mantle — and strikes the water himself. It parts. The watching prophets recognize what has happened: "The spirit of Elijah rests on Elisha."

God's voice does not depend on any one prophet. When Elijah goes, Elisha continues. When Elisha eventually dies, the writing prophets begin. The voice keeps speaking.
days.plain_english_deeper:
Today's reading establishes the prophetic office and introduces two of the most theologically significant prophets in the Hebrew Bible. Several features deepen the reading.

**The Hebrew prophetic office.** The word *nabi* (prophet) is best understood through its verbal pairing with God's act of *sending*. A prophet is one whom God sends with a message. The prophet's authority is not personal charisma but the message itself — which is why the prophets often introduce their oracles with "thus says Yahweh." Deuteronomy 18:15-22 establishes the formal criteria: a true prophet speaks what God has commanded, and what he predicts comes to pass. False prophets — speaking on behalf of other gods or fabricating in Yahweh's name — were to be put to death (Deut 18:20).

Functionally, prophets in the Hebrew Bible perform three overlapping roles:
  1. *Covenant prosecutors* — calling God's people back to the terms of the covenant they had broken
  2. *Foretellers* — announcing what God would do, both in judgment and in restoration
  3. *Sign-actors* — sometimes performing dramatic actions (Hosea marrying an unfaithful wife, Ezekiel lying on his side for over a year) that embodied the message

Elijah and Elisha fit primarily into the first role, with strong sign-acting components.

**Historical setting of Mount Carmel.** The contest at Carmel takes place during the reign of King Ahab of Israel (the northern kingdom) — generally dated to around 870-852 BC. Ahab married Jezebel, daughter of the Sidonian king Ethbaal. Jezebel imported the worship of Baal-Melqart, the patron deity of Tyre and Sidon. She systematically persecuted Yahweh's prophets (1 Kings 18:4 notes that Obadiah hid one hundred of them in caves to spare their lives). Elijah's claim to be "the only prophet of Yahweh left" is hyperbole reflecting his isolation; he knew of Obadiah's hidden prophets but was alone in the public confrontation.

The choice of Mount Carmel is significant. Carmel is a fertile coastal promontory, traditionally regarded as Baal's stronghold. Elijah challenges Baal on Baal's home territory.

**The mockery of Baal.** Elijah's taunts in verse 27 are theologically as well as rhetorically pointed. Each accusation undermines Baal's claimed divinity. "He is musing" or "on a journey" — gods who travel and are absent are not omnipresent. "He sleeps and must be awakened" — gods who sleep are not omniscient or sovereign. The Hebrew euphemism that may underlie "gone aside" (relieving himself) is the sharpest: gods with bodily functions are not gods at all. The prophet exposes the rival deity by reductio ad absurdum.

**The repaired altar and twelve stones.** Elijah's choice to use twelve stones (verse 31) is theologically loaded. By 870 BC the kingdom had been divided for about sixty years; the ten northern tribes had separated from the two southern tribes. By gathering twelve stones, Elijah is enacting a prophetic vision: the people of God are *still one nation in God's sight*, regardless of political division. The altar he builds is not a northern-kingdom altar; it is *Israel's* altar.

**The drowning of the offering.** Pouring twelve jars of water on the sacrifice was not theatrics for theatrics' sake. Water was precious during the drought Elijah had announced (1 Kings 17:1; 18:5). To pour out the limited water supply demonstrated total reliance on Yahweh. It also removed any possibility of accidental ignition, making the fire from heaven unambiguous.

**Elijah's translation.** Elijah's removal from earth by whirlwind is one of two such accounts in Scripture; the other is Enoch (Genesis 5:24). Both men are described as walking with God in such a way that death is bypassed. The New Testament treats Elijah's translation as a real historical event (Matthew 17:3 places him alive at the Transfiguration alongside Moses).

The "chariot of fire and horses of fire" recall the imagery of God's heavenly armies that recur throughout the Hebrew Bible (2 Kings 6:17 explicitly identifies them as Yahweh's hosts). Elisha's exclamation — "the chariots of Israel and its horsemen!" — is later applied to Elisha himself when he dies (2 Kings 13:14): the true strength of Israel is not in its cavalry but in its prophets.

**Elijah in Jewish and Christian expectation.** Because Elijah did not die, post-biblical Jewish tradition expected him to return as a herald of the Messiah (rooted in Malachi 4:5-6, which closes the Old Testament — and which we'll read on Day 7). The New Testament identifies John the Baptist as fulfilling this role "in the spirit and power of Elijah" (Luke 1:17), and Jesus explicitly confirms it (Matthew 11:14; 17:12). The cloak passed to Elisha at the Jordan thus foreshadows a much larger pattern: God's voice gets handed forward.
days.key_insight: A prophet in the Bible is God's spokesperson when the kings fail — not a fortune-teller. The first question a prophet asks is always the same: how long will you waver?
days.reflection_prompt: Where in your life are you "limping between two sides" — half-committed to God and half-committed to something else? What would it look like to stop limping today?
days.application_action: Name one small "Baal" in your life — one thing you've been trying to honor alongside God. Write it down. Pray over it. Ask God to help you stop wavering.

confusion_topics.topic: What is a prophet, really? Is it just someone who predicts the future?
confusion_topics.plain_english_answer: No — prediction is a small part of the job. The Hebrew word for prophet (*nabi*) means roughly 'spokesperson.' A prophet speaks for God to people, especially when those people have drifted. Prophets sometimes predicted future events, but they spent far more time calling God's people back to the covenant they had broken. Think of them as the conscience of a forgetful nation, not as crystal-ball readers. When the kings stop listening to God, the prophets are God's way of still being heard.

confusion_topics.topic: Why are the prophets in such a confusing order in my Bible?
confusion_topics.plain_english_answer: Great question, and a frustration almost every reader has. The prophetic books are NOT in chronological order. They're grouped by LENGTH — the longer ones (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Daniel) are called 'major prophets,' and the shorter ones (Hosea through Malachi) are called 'minor prophets.' 'Minor' just means shorter, not less important. To follow the story chronologically, you'd read them in roughly this order: Amos and Hosea (~750 BC, northern kingdom), Isaiah and Micah (~740 BC, southern kingdom), Jeremiah (~620 BC, just before exile), Ezekiel and Daniel (during exile in Babylon), and finally Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi (after the return). This week we'll walk them in roughly that order.

confusion_topics.topic: Was Elijah really taken up to heaven without dying?
confusion_topics.plain_english_answer: Yes — the Bible records two people who skipped death: Enoch in Genesis 5 ('he walked with God, and he was not, for God took him'), and Elijah here in 2 Kings 2. The New Testament treats Elijah's translation as a real historical event — Matthew 17 records Jesus' Transfiguration, where Elijah appears alongside Moses, alive. Because Elijah didn't die, Jewish tradition (rooted in Malachi 4:5-6) expected him to return before the Day of the Lord. Jesus said John the Baptist fulfilled that role 'in the spirit and power of Elijah' (Luke 1:17).

confusion_topics.topic: Why does Elijah kill the prophets of Baal at the end? That seems harsh.
confusion_topics.plain_english_answer: It does to modern ears, and it's worth sitting with. A few things to know: (1) The prophets of Baal had been actively involved in killing Yahweh's prophets under Queen Jezebel's persecution — this wasn't unprovoked. (2) The Mosaic Law in Deuteronomy 13 and 18 commanded the death of false prophets who tried to lead Israel into worshiping other gods, because such worship would destroy the nation. (3) The scene records what Elijah did, not necessarily what God prescribed for all time — the New Testament under Christ explicitly redirects God's people away from physical violence and toward spiritual warfare (Ephesians 6:12, 2 Corinthians 10:4). The Old Testament is honest about its hard moments; it does not soften them.

days.retention_anchor: Yesterday's arc ended with the kingdom split and most of the kings failing. Today you met the other voice God uses when kings go wrong: the prophet. Elijah set the template — uncompromising, sometimes lonely, calling people to stop wavering. Tomorrow we move to the first of the writing prophets, Isaiah, and a vision of God so holy it shakes the foundations.

blocks.text: In the year that king Uzziah died, I saw the Lord sitting on a throne, high and lifted up; and his train filled the temple.
Above him stood the seraphim. Each one had six wings. With two he covered his face. With two he covered his feet. With two he flew.
One called to another, and said, "Holy, holy, holy, is Yahweh of Armies! The whole earth is full of his glory!"
The foundations of the thresholds shook at the voice of him who called, and the house was filled with smoke.
Then I said, "Woe is me! For I am undone, because I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell among a people of unclean lips: for my eyes have seen the King, Yahweh of Armies!"
Then one of the seraphim flew to me, having a live coal in his hand, which he had taken with the tongs from off the altar.
He touched my mouth with it, and said, "Behold, this has touched your lips; and your iniquity is taken away, and your sin forgiven."
I heard the Lord's voice, saying, "Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?" Then I said, "Here I am. Send me!"
Who has believed our message? To whom has Yahweh's arm been revealed?
For he grew up before him as a tender plant, and as a root out of dry ground. He has no good looks or majesty. When we see him, there is no beauty that we should desire him.
He was despised and rejected by men, a man of suffering and acquainted with disease. He was despised as one from whom men hide their face; and we didn't respect him.
Surely he has borne our sickness and carried our suffering; yet we considered him plagued, struck by God, and afflicted.
But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed.
All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all.
He was oppressed, yet when he was afflicted he didn't open his mouth. As a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and as a sheep that before its shearers is silent, so he didn't open his mouth.
He was taken away by oppression and judgment. As for his generation, who among them considered that he was cut off out of the land of the living and stricken for the disobedience of my people?
They made his grave with the wicked, and with a rich man in his death, although he had done no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth.

Yet it pleased Yahweh to bruise him. He has caused him to suffer. When you make his soul an offering for sin, he will see his offspring. He will prolong his days and Yahweh's pleasure will prosper in his hand.
After the suffering of his soul, he will see the light and be satisfied. My righteous servant will justify many by the knowledge of himself; and he will bear their iniquities.

Therefore I will give him a portion with the great. He will divide the plunder with the strong; because he poured out his soul to death and was counted with the transgressors; yet he bore the sins of many and made intercession for the transgressors.

days.context_before:
Yesterday Elijah stood on a mountain and called fire from heaven. Today you'll meet Isaiah — the first of the prophets who wrote down their messages — and read two of the most famous passages in the Old Testament.

Isaiah ministered in the southern kingdom of Judah for around fifty years. The northern kingdom (Israel) was sliding toward its destruction by Assyria in 722 BC; Judah was being warned not to follow. Isaiah is the longest prophetic book in the Bible (66 chapters), and he speaks to almost every theme that matters: God's holiness, judgment, mercy, the coming Messiah, the new creation.

We'll read two passages today. The first (Isaiah 6) is the prophet's call — a vision in the temple of God on his throne, and Isaiah's response. The second (Isaiah 53) is a passage written roughly seven hundred years before Jesus that Christians for two thousand years have read and seen Jesus on every line.

Watch for the threefold cry of the angels: "Holy, holy, holy." In Hebrew, repeating a word emphasizes it; repeating it three times makes it superlative. God is not just holy. He is holy to the maximum that language can describe.
days.plain_english_simple:
Isaiah's vision begins with a date — the year King Uzziah died, about 740 BC. Uzziah had been one of Judah's better kings, and his death left the nation anxious. In that moment, Isaiah sees something far bigger than a kingdom changing hands. He sees the Lord on a throne, with angels (called seraphim) covering their faces because the sight is too much.

The angels cry: "Holy, holy, holy." Three times. The whole temple shakes.

Isaiah's reaction is honest. He doesn't feel inspired or excited. He feels undone. "Woe is me!" He sees a holy God and feels his own uncleanness. An angel takes a burning coal from the altar and touches Isaiah's lips — and his sin is forgiven.

Then God asks: "Whom shall I send?" Isaiah volunteers: "Here I am. Send me."

The second passage jumps forty-seven chapters ahead — to Isaiah 53. It describes a strange, suffering figure called the "Servant of the Lord." He's despised. Rejected. A man of sorrows. He carries the sicknesses and sins of others. He's pierced for our wrongs. He's silent like a lamb led to slaughter. He dies — and then somehow he is satisfied, his work prospers, and many are made right with God through him.

Written roughly seven hundred years before Jesus, Christians have read this chapter for two thousand years and seen one face on every line.
days.plain_english_standard:
Isaiah ministered in the southern kingdom of Judah from about 740 BC to roughly 680 BC — a span of around sixty years, across the reigns of four kings. The northern kingdom was crumbling under Assyrian pressure (it would fall in 722 BC). Isaiah's call was to warn Judah not to follow the same path.

**The vision in the temple (Isaiah 6).** The vision is dated to "the year that King Uzziah died" — about 740 BC. Uzziah had reigned for fifty-two years; his death created national anxiety about the future. Into that anxiety, Isaiah sees what really sits on the throne: not a human king, but the Lord, "high and lifted up."

The seraphim — six-winged beings — cover their faces. Even sinless angels cannot look directly at God. They cover their feet (a posture of humility). And they fly.

Their cry is the central thing: "Holy, holy, holy, is Yahweh of Armies!" In Hebrew, repetition is the way you emphasize. Saying something twice means it's extreme. Saying it three times means it's at the absolute maximum. There is no fourth-degree holy in Hebrew. The seraphim are saying: this God is as holy as language can describe.

Isaiah's reaction is the right one. He doesn't feel inspired. He feels undone. "Woe is me!" — the same word the prophets use when pronouncing curses. Isaiah pronounces it on himself. In the blazing presence of holiness, he sees his own unclean speech, and his people's, and knows it cannot stand.

An angel takes a live coal from the altar and touches Isaiah's lips. "Your iniquity is taken away, and your sin forgiven." This is one of the most important sequences in the Bible: vision of holiness, awareness of sin, divine cleansing, *then* commissioning. God does not send unclean messengers. He cleans them first.

Only then does God ask: "Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?" And Isaiah — the cleansed Isaiah — answers: "Here I am. Send me."

**The Suffering Servant (Isaiah 53).** Now we jump forty-seven chapters. Isaiah 40-55 contains four passages called the "Servant Songs," describing a mysterious figure called the Servant of the Lord. Isaiah 52:13 - 53:12 is the fourth and most famous. It describes a Servant who:

- Is despised and rejected by people
- Carries our sickness and our suffering
- Is pierced for our transgressions and crushed for our iniquities
- Is silent like a lamb led to slaughter
- Is buried with the wicked and a rich man in his death
- Dies as an offering for sin
- *And then* sees "his offspring," "prolongs his days," is "satisfied," and makes many righteous

The pattern is shocking even read on its own terms: a righteous servant suffers and dies on behalf of others, and somehow lives to see the fruit of it. The Hebrew text gives no clear earthly identity for this servant.

Written roughly seven hundred years before Jesus, this chapter is one of the foundational reasons Christians read the Hebrew Bible as pointing forward to Christ. Every line — the rejection, the silence at trial, the bearing of others' sin, the burial with the rich, the death between transgressors, the seeing of offspring after death — fits Jesus' story so precisely that the New Testament cites Isaiah 53 more than almost any other Hebrew passage (see Matthew 8:17, Mark 15:28, Luke 22:37, John 12:38, Acts 8:32-35, Romans 10:16, 1 Peter 2:22-25).

For this journey, we are reading Isaiah 53 in the way Christians have read it for two thousand years: as a prophecy of Jesus, who fulfilled the role of the Suffering Servant on the cross.

Isaiah saw the King in his holiness. Then, looking forward across centuries, Isaiah also saw the King in his suffering.
days.plain_english_deeper:
Isaiah is one of the most theologically dense books in the Hebrew Bible. Today's two passages establish themes that will run through the New Testament.

**Historical setting.** Isaiah ben Amoz ministered in Jerusalem from approximately 740 BC to roughly 680 BC, spanning the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah (Isaiah 1:1). His ministry overlapped with the Assyrian expansion that destroyed the northern kingdom of Israel in 722 BC and besieged Jerusalem in 701 BC. The early chapters of Isaiah address the political crisis of Assyrian threat; the later chapters (40-66) speak comfort and restoration to a community that would still be over a century from exile.

**The throne vision (Isaiah 6).** The vision's location — "in the year that King Uzziah died" — is theologically significant. Uzziah had reigned fifty-two years, longer than most kings, providing political stability. His death (around 740 BC) marked a generational transition under the looming shadow of Assyria. Isaiah's vision insists that the *real* throne is never empty.

The Hebrew word translated "Lord" in 6:1 is *Adonai* (the title used as a substitute for the divine name). The seraphim's title for God in verse 3 is *Yahweh Sabaoth* — "Yahweh of armies" or "Lord of hosts" — emphasizing his command of the heavenly armies. In a moment when an earthly king has just died, Isaiah sees the unchanging cosmic King.

**"Holy, holy, holy."** The threefold *qadosh, qadosh, qadosh* is the only place in the Hebrew Bible where any divine attribute is repeated three times. Repetition in Hebrew is intensification: doubling means emphatic, tripling means superlative. God is not merely holy; he is holy to the absolute maximum that language can express. Christian theology has often read this threefold cry as a hint of the Trinity, though the text does not explicitly require that reading; the more immediate point is the absolute, peerless holiness of God.

The word *qadosh* (holy) means "set apart" or "separate." God is holy not merely in the sense of being morally pure, but in being categorically *other* — utterly distinct from creation. Isaiah's reaction ("I am undone") is the only appropriate human response to that kind of holiness.

**The burning coal.** The altar from which the coal is taken is the altar of burnt offering — where sacrifices were consumed. The coal carries the fire of sacrifice; touching it to Isaiah's lips applies the cleansing of sacrifice to his speech. This is a prophetic foreshadowing: cleansing of sin will ultimately come through a sacrifice. Isaiah does not yet see how complete that sacrifice will be, but the seed is here.

**The commissioning.** The structure of Isaiah 6 — theophany, conviction of sin, cleansing, commissioning — is a recognizable biblical pattern. It echoes Moses at the burning bush (Exodus 3) and anticipates Paul's experience on the Damascus road (Acts 9). God does not press uncleansed people into service. He cleans, then sends.

**The Servant Songs.** Isaiah 40-55 (a section often called "Second Isaiah" in scholarly literature, though traditional Christian and Jewish interpretation has read all 66 chapters as the work of the one prophet Isaiah) contains four distinct passages about a figure called "the Servant of Yahweh":
  - Isaiah 42:1-9 — The Servant is gentle, just, a light to the nations
  - Isaiah 49:1-7 — The Servant gathers Israel and is a light to the Gentiles
  - Isaiah 50:4-9 — The Servant suffers willingly, trusting God to vindicate him
  - Isaiah 52:13 - 53:12 — The Servant suffers and dies vicariously, then is exalted

**Who is the Servant?** Within Isaiah itself, the term "servant" sometimes refers to Israel as a nation (Isaiah 41:8, 44:1). But in the Servant Songs — especially Isaiah 53 — the Servant is clearly distinct from Israel and suffers *on behalf of* Israel and the nations. Jewish interpretation has historically wrestled with this tension; some readings identify the Servant as Israel collectively suffering, others as a coming individual deliverer.

The New Testament identifies the Suffering Servant unambiguously as Jesus. Acts 8 records the Ethiopian eunuch reading Isaiah 53 and asking Philip, "About whom does the prophet say this?" Philip answers by preaching Jesus from that passage. The early church saw Isaiah 53 as one of the clearest Old Testament prefigurations of the cross.

**Substitutionary atonement.** The vocabulary of Isaiah 53 is theologically precise. Verse 5: "He was *pierced for* our transgressions. He was *crushed for* our iniquities. The punishment that brought *our peace was on him*." Verse 6: "Yahweh has *laid on him* the iniquity of us all." Verse 10: "His soul [is] an offering for sin." The grammar consistently uses substitutionary prepositions: the Servant suffers in place of and on behalf of others, and his suffering accomplishes their peace. This is the Old Testament foundation for what the New Testament calls "atonement" — Christ's death in the place of sinners.

**"He will see his offspring."** Verse 10 contains a quiet but stunning detail: the Servant dies, and *then* he sees his offspring, prolongs his days, and is satisfied. This implies that death is not the end for the Servant. The text does not use the word "resurrection," but the logic requires that the Servant who dies in the middle of the chapter is somehow alive at the end of it. The New Testament reads this as Isaiah's anticipation of the resurrection of Christ.
days.key_insight: Isaiah saw God so holy the temple shook — and then, looking forward, saw a Servant who would bear our sin and die in our place. Both visions are about the same God.
days.reflection_prompt: When you imagine standing before a holy God, do you tend to come with confidence in yourself, or do you come like Isaiah — undone? What might it look like to receive the burning coal of forgiveness today?
days.application_action: Spend two minutes in silence today picturing Isaiah's scene. Whisper back the angels' words: 'Holy, holy, holy.' Then receive God's forgiveness — and say 'Here I am.'

confusion_topics.topic: Why does the angel say 'holy' three times? Is that important?
confusion_topics.plain_english_answer: Yes — and Hebrew readers would have caught it immediately. In Hebrew, you emphasize a word by repeating it. Saying something twice is emphatic; saying it three times is superlative. There's no fourth-degree 'holy' in Hebrew. The seraphim are saying: this God is as holy as language can express. Isaiah 6 is the only place in the Hebrew Bible where any divine attribute gets tripled. Some Christians have also seen in the threefold cry a hint of the Trinity (Father, Son, Spirit — one God), though the main point is the absolute, peerless holiness of God.

confusion_topics.topic: Isaiah 53 sounds exactly like Jesus. Was it really written 700 years before him?
confusion_topics.plain_english_answer: Yes. Isaiah ministered around 740-680 BC. The Dead Sea Scrolls discovered in 1947 included a complete copy of Isaiah dated to about 125 BC — that's more than a century BEFORE Jesus was born. We have hard physical evidence that Isaiah 53 existed, in essentially its modern form, well before Christ. Christians for 2,000 years have read it and seen Jesus on every line: rejection, silence at trial, suffering, pierced for others, buried with the rich, dying with transgressors, then somehow seeing 'offspring' after death. The New Testament quotes Isaiah 53 more than almost any other Hebrew passage. The Ethiopian official in Acts 8 was literally reading Isaiah 53 when Philip walked up and explained that the passage was about Jesus.

confusion_topics.topic: Who is the 'Suffering Servant'? Is it Israel, or Jesus, or both?
confusion_topics.plain_english_answer: Within Isaiah, the word 'servant' sometimes refers to the nation of Israel collectively (Isaiah 41:8). But in Isaiah 53 specifically, the Servant is clearly a person who suffers and dies ON BEHALF OF others — including Israel itself. So the Servant in Isaiah 53 cannot simply BE Israel; he suffers FOR Israel. Jewish interpretation has wrestled with this passage in different ways. The Christian reading, going back to Jesus himself and the New Testament writers, is that the Suffering Servant is Jesus, fulfilling the role no human nation could fulfill. The passage was foundational to how the early church understood the cross.

confusion_topics.topic: What's the difference between 'major' and 'minor' prophets?
confusion_topics.plain_english_answer: Just length. The 'major prophets' (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Lamentations, Ezekiel, Daniel) are the long books. The 'minor prophets' (Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi — twelve in total) are the short ones. The category has nothing to do with importance. Some of the most stunning prophetic lines in the Bible come from 'minor' prophets — Micah's 'do justly, love mercy, walk humbly' is a single verse longer than some entire chapters of Isaiah. On Day 6 we'll sample several of the minor prophets together.

days.retention_anchor: Yesterday Elijah faced Baal on a mountain. Today Isaiah faced the holy God in the temple — and saw, centuries early, the Servant who would suffer for our sin. Tomorrow you meet Jeremiah, the prophet who wept as he watched the southern kingdom slide toward the destruction Isaiah warned about. By Day 4, the exile is happening.

"Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you. Before you were born, I sanctified you. I have appointed you a prophet to the nations."
Then I said, "Ah, Lord Yahweh! Behold, I don't know how to speak; for I am a child."
But Yahweh said to me, "Don't say, 'I am a child;' for you must go to whomever I shall send you, and you must say whatever I shall command you.
Don't be afraid because of them, for I am with you to rescue you," says Yahweh.
Then Yahweh stretched out his hand and touched my mouth. Then Yahweh said to me, "Behold, I have put my words in your mouth.
Behold, I have today set you over the nations and over the kingdoms, to uproot and to tear down and to destroy and to overthrow, to build and to plant."
"Behold, the days come," says Yahweh, "that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel, and with the house of Judah:

not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers in the day that I took them by the hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt, which covenant of mine they broke, although I was a husband to them," says Yahweh.

"But this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days," says Yahweh: "I will put my law in their inward parts, and I will write it in their heart. I will be their God, and they shall be my people.

They will no longer each teach his neighbor, and every man teach his brother, saying, 'Know Yahweh;' for they will all know me, from their least to their greatest," says Yahweh: "for I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more."

days.context_before:
Roughly a hundred years pass between Isaiah and Jeremiah. Isaiah's warnings about Judah were not heeded; the nation has continued to slide. Now Jeremiah is called — and his job is harder than Isaiah's, because there's no longer time to turn the ship around. He will live to see Jerusalem destroyed by Babylon.

Jeremiah ministered from about 626 BC until just after the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC — roughly forty years of preaching what almost nobody wanted to hear. He's often called 'the weeping prophet' because his book is wet with grief over his people.

Today's reading shows two things: his call (Jeremiah 1) and his most stunning promise (Jeremiah 31). The call begins with a startling sentence — God formed him for this before he was born. The promise looks past all the judgment and announces something brand new: a covenant written not on stone but on hearts. Jesus quotes this passage at the Last Supper. It's that important.

Watch for the contrast: Jeremiah is going to deliver a message of doom, and yet inside that message is the seed of the greatest hope in the Old Testament.
days.plain_english_simple:
Jeremiah's call begins with words that should stop you in your tracks: 'Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you. Before you were born, I sanctified you.' God knew Jeremiah and chose his job before Jeremiah existed.

Jeremiah is not thrilled. He protests: 'I don't know how to speak. I'm just a child.' God answers: 'Don't say that. Go where I send you. Say what I tell you. I am with you.' Then God touches his mouth and puts his words in it.

Jeremiah's calling has six verbs in it (verse 10): to uproot, to tear down, to destroy, to overthrow — and then to build, and to plant. Four verbs of judgment, two of restoration. That's roughly the shape of his book. The destruction is real. So is what comes after.

Then we jump to chapter 31 — Jeremiah's most famous promise. God says he will make a 'new covenant' with his people. Not like the old one, written on stone tablets that they kept breaking. This one will be written on their hearts. Everyone will know God personally. And God will forgive their sin and remember it no more.

Seven hundred years later, on the night before he died, Jesus picked up a cup at the last supper and said: 'This is my blood of the new covenant.' He was quoting Jeremiah 31. The promise God made through a weeping prophet is the promise Jesus came to keep.
days.plain_english_standard:
Jeremiah ministered from about 626 BC to just after the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC — roughly forty years of preaching judgment to a nation that did not want to hear it. He was born into a priestly family in Anathoth, a village a few miles north of Jerusalem. He came to be called 'the weeping prophet' because his book — and a separate book named Lamentations, traditionally attributed to him — is soaked with grief over his people.

**The call (Jeremiah 1:4-10).** Jeremiah's call narrative is one of the most personal in the Bible. God says: 'Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you. Before you were born, I sanctified you. I have appointed you a prophet to the nations.'

Three things stand out:
  1. *Before I formed you* — God's knowing of Jeremiah preceded Jeremiah's existence
  2. *I sanctified you* — God set Jeremiah apart for this work; the choice was not Jeremiah's
  3. *To the nations* — Jeremiah's audience is bigger than Judah; he'll speak God's word about Egypt, Moab, Babylon, and others

Jeremiah's response is the same as Moses' (Exodus 4) and many other called servants: 'I'm not qualified.' He pleads his age — the Hebrew word *na'ar* could mean anything from a child to a young man, but the point is he feels too young.

God's answer is patient. He doesn't argue. He simply overrides the objection: 'Don't say, I am a child.' He commissions Jeremiah to go where sent and speak what is given — and promises his presence.

Then God touches Jeremiah's mouth (a deliberate echo of Isaiah's call) and places his words there. The six verbs in verse 10 — uproot, tear down, destroy, overthrow, build, plant — define Jeremiah's prophetic vocation. Four verbs of judgment, two of restoration. The shape of his ministry will be more demolition than construction, but the construction is real.

**Forty years of pain.** It's worth pausing on what Jeremiah's life actually looked like. He preached for four decades to a hostile audience. He was beaten and put in stocks (Jeremiah 20). He was threatened with death by the priests and prophets (Jeremiah 26). His scroll was cut up and burned by the king (Jeremiah 36). He was lowered into a muddy cistern and left to die (Jeremiah 38). When Jerusalem finally fell in 586 BC, he was forcibly taken to Egypt against his will. Through all of it, he never stopped preaching.

Most prophets had at least *some* people listen. Jeremiah, by his own testimony, was almost universally rejected. And yet — this is the wonder — into the bleakest book in the Old Testament, God planted one of the greatest promises in all of Scripture.

**The new covenant (Jeremiah 31:31-34).** Chapter 31 sits in a small island of hope within the larger book — chapters 30-33 are sometimes called the 'Book of Consolation.' Jeremiah, who has spent most of his life prophesying disaster, is given a vision of what God will do *after* the disaster.

The key phrase is *new covenant*. God says he will make a new covenant with his people — not like the one made at Sinai (the one with Moses, written on stone tablets, the one the people kept breaking). This new covenant will have four features:

  1. **Internal** — God will put his law inside his people, written on their hearts, not on external tablets they can ignore
  2. **Relational** — 'I will be their God, and they shall be my people' (the covenant formula that runs through the whole Bible)
  3. **Personal** — every individual will know God directly, from the least to the greatest, without needing to be taught by another
  4. **Forgiving** — 'I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more'

This is the highest theological promise in the Hebrew Bible.

**Jesus picks up the cup.** Seven hundred years later, on the night before his death, Jesus held up a cup at the Last Supper and said: 'This cup is the new covenant in my blood' (Luke 22:20; see also 1 Corinthians 11:25 and Hebrews 8:8-12, which quotes Jeremiah 31 in full). Jesus was deliberately, explicitly identifying his death as the fulfillment of Jeremiah's promise. The new covenant is what the cross inaugurates.

For this journey, we are reading Jeremiah 31 as a direct prophecy that finds its fulfillment in Jesus and the gospel — the way Jesus himself read it, the way the New Testament reads it, the way Christians have read it for two thousand years.

A weeping prophet, faithfully preaching to people who would not listen, was given the promise that would change the world.
days.plain_english_deeper:
Jeremiah is one of the longest books in the Bible and one of the most emotionally raw. Today's two passages anchor his call and his greatest contribution.

**Historical setting.** Jeremiah ben Hilkiah was born in Anathoth (a Levitical village three miles north of Jerusalem) into a priestly family probably descended from Abiathar, whom Solomon had banished from temple service. He was called to prophesy in the thirteenth year of King Josiah (Jeremiah 1:2) — approximately 626 BC. His ministry spanned the reigns of five kings: Josiah, Jehoahaz, Jehoiakim, Jehoiachin, and Zedekiah. He lived through Josiah's reforms (which were too late and too shallow to reverse the spiritual decay), the death of Josiah at Megiddo in 609 BC, the rise of Babylon, the first deportation in 597 BC (which took Daniel and Ezekiel), the final destruction of Jerusalem in 586 BC, and the subsequent flight of survivors to Egypt — where Jeremiah died, by tradition murdered by his own people.

**The pre-natal calling.** Jeremiah 1:5 is one of the most theologically loaded verses in the prophetic literature. The verbs are precise:
  - *I knew you* (*yada*) — not mere intellectual awareness; the Hebrew verb implies relational, covenantal knowledge
  - *I sanctified you* (*qadash*) — set apart for sacred purpose
  - *I appointed you* (*natan*) — literally 'gave' you as a prophet

The sequence shows that Jeremiah's role was God-initiated, not chosen. This is consistent across biblical calling narratives (Moses, Isaiah, Paul) — those whom God calls do not select the role; the role selects them.

**The 'I am a child' objection.** Jeremiah's protest in 1:6 ('I am a child') uses the Hebrew *na'ar*, which can refer to anyone from infancy to roughly age thirty. Jeremiah was likely in his late teens or early twenties at his call. His objection echoes Moses' protest of inadequate speech (Exodus 4:10) and is met with the same response: God's presence and provision, not the prophet's qualifications, are what matter.

**The six verbs.** Jeremiah 1:10 sets the agenda for the entire book with six verbs:
  - *Uproot* (*natash*) — to pull out by the roots
  - *Tear down* (*natats*) — to demolish a structure
  - *Destroy* (*abad*) — to cause to perish
  - *Overthrow* (*haras*) — to throw down
  - *Build* (*banah*) — to construct
  - *Plant* (*nata*) — to set into the soil

Four verbs of demolition, two of construction. The ratio reflects Jeremiah's vocation: most of his ministry was warning of judgment, but the judgment was never the final word. After the demolition, God would build and plant. This shape — judgment that clears space for genuine restoration — runs through the entire prophetic literature.

**Jeremiah's suffering.** The book includes several extended passages called the 'Confessions of Jeremiah' (Jeremiah 11:18-23; 12:1-6; 15:10-21; 17:14-18; 18:18-23; 20:7-18), in which Jeremiah pours out his anguish to God. He accuses God of deceiving him (20:7), curses the day of his birth (20:14-18), and complains that he cannot stop preaching even though preaching has destroyed his life. No other prophetic book is so personally autobiographical. The Hebrew Bible does not pretend that being God's spokesperson was easy.

**Lamentations.** Traditionally attributed to Jeremiah, the book of Lamentations is a five-chapter funeral poem for fallen Jerusalem. Its central chapter (Lamentations 3) contains the famous lines, 'It is of Yahweh's loving kindnesses that we are not consumed... they are new every morning' (3:22-23). Even in the deepest national grief, the prophet's faith in God's covenant love does not break.

**The new covenant in context.** Jeremiah 30-33 forms a discrete section often called the 'Book of Consolation' — a concentrated burst of restoration prophecy embedded in an otherwise dark book. Chapter 31:31-34 is its theological climax.

The Hebrew phrase *berit chadashah* ('new covenant') appears only here in the Hebrew Bible. The word *chadash* means 'new' in the sense of fresh, qualitatively different, not merely chronologically later. The new covenant is not a renewed Mosaic covenant; it is a different kind of covenant.

**Four features of the new covenant:**
  1. *Internal* (verse 33) — 'I will put my law in their inward parts, and I will write it in their heart.' The Mosaic covenant was external — written on tablets, depending on human obedience to remain intact. The new covenant is internal — written on hearts, divinely implanted.
  2. *Relational* (verse 33) — 'I will be their God, and they shall be my people.' This is the covenant formula present from Genesis to Revelation. The new covenant fulfills it definitively.
  3. *Personal* (verse 34) — 'They will no longer each teach his neighbor... saying, Know Yahweh; for they will all know me, from their least to their greatest.' Under the old covenant, knowing God was mediated through priests and teachers; under the new, every believer has direct knowledge of God.
  4. *Forgiving* (verse 34) — 'I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more.' Forgiveness in the old covenant required repeated sacrifices; the new covenant offers definitive, remembered-no-more forgiveness.

**New Testament fulfillment.** Jesus' words at the Last Supper — 'This is my blood of the new covenant' (Matthew 26:28; Mark 14:24; Luke 22:20; 1 Corinthians 11:25) — explicitly identify his death as the inauguration of Jeremiah's new covenant. The book of Hebrews quotes Jeremiah 31:31-34 in full (Hebrews 8:8-12; 10:16-17) and develops the theology at length: the new covenant has come, the old has been superseded, and what Jeremiah promised is now experienced by all who trust in Christ.

The weeping prophet, whose forty-year ministry seemed to fail on its own terms, was given the promise that defines Christian faith. The book that documents catastrophic national failure contains the seed of the gospel.
days.key_insight: Jeremiah wept his way through forty years of unheeded warnings — and was given the promise of a covenant written on hearts that Jesus would later inaugurate at the Last Supper.
days.reflection_prompt: What does it mean to you that God knew you before you were formed in the womb — and what would it look like to live today as someone called and known, not random?
days.application_action: Read Jeremiah 31:33 out loud, slowly, twice. Then thank God for one specific way his law has been written on YOUR heart — a value, an instinct, a love for what is right.

confusion_topics.topic: What's a 'covenant'? And what makes the 'new covenant' new?
confusion_topics.plain_english_answer: A covenant in the Bible is a formal, binding relationship — usually with promises, obligations, and signs. God made several covenants in the Old Testament: with Noah (a promise never to flood the earth again), with Abraham (a promise of land and descendants), and with Moses at Sinai (the law, written on stone tablets, with promised blessings for obedience and consequences for disobedience). The 'new' covenant Jeremiah promised is qualitatively different. The Sinai covenant was external — God's law written on tablets, kept by human effort, broken constantly. The new covenant is internal — God's law written on hearts, with sins forgiven and forgotten, and every believer knowing God personally. Jesus said at the Last Supper that his blood was the blood of this new covenant — meaning the cross is what makes Jeremiah's promise come true.

confusion_topics.topic: Why does God let the exile happen if Israel is his chosen people?
confusion_topics.plain_english_answer: It's one of the hardest questions in the Old Testament — and the prophets address it directly. The answer is essentially this: being God's chosen people came with covenant obligations (read Deuteronomy 28). God had promised blessings for faithfulness and consequences for repeated, generational unfaithfulness. Israel had spent centuries worshiping other gods, oppressing the poor, ignoring God's law, and killing the prophets sent to warn them. The exile was not God abandoning his people — it was God taking seriously the covenant they had broken. And here's the key thing: the exile was never the end. The prophets who announced the exile (like Jeremiah) ALSO announced the return. The discipline was designed to bring God's people back, not to destroy them. God's love and God's justice are not opposites in the Bible — they work together.

confusion_topics.topic: Was Jeremiah really called before he was born? Does that mean God plans everything?
confusion_topics.plain_english_answer: Jeremiah 1:5 says God knew and chose Jeremiah before he was formed in the womb. Christian traditions have wrestled with how this works in tension with human free will, and they don't all answer it the same way. The text itself is making a specific claim about Jeremiah's prophetic call: God personally appointed him for this role before he existed, so the calling didn't depend on Jeremiah's qualifications or choice. Other passages (Psalm 139, Ephesians 1) extend similar language to all of God's people. The takeaway for you: you are not an accident. The God who knew Jeremiah knew you. Whatever else you puzzle out about how God's sovereignty and human freedom interact, you can rest in being known.

confusion_topics.topic: How does prophecy 'work'? Did Jeremiah literally hear God's voice?
confusion_topics.plain_english_answer: The prophets describe their experience of receiving God's word in different ways. Sometimes it's a clear inner word ('the word of Yahweh came to me'). Sometimes it's a vision (Isaiah in the temple, Ezekiel by the river). Sometimes it's a dream. Sometimes it's a dramatic sign-action they're commanded to perform. What's consistent is that the prophets distinguished sharply between their own thoughts and the message God gave them — and they were willing to suffer for the message even when they themselves found it painful. The New Testament summary is: 'No prophecy ever came by the will of man; but men spoke from God, being moved by the Holy Spirit' (2 Peter 1:21). The exact experience varied; the source was the same.

Today Jeremiah was called before birth — to weep through forty years of unheeded warnings and yet to deliver the promise of the new covenant Jesus would later seal in his blood. Tomorrow the exile actually happens. We move to Babylon, where Ezekiel — exiled with the first deportation — sees a valley of dry bones come back to life.
